To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) The expression of NK receptors and the NK activities of HIV‐infected individuals with the highest plasma viral load were decreased, and vice versa.
NK activity of the AIDS patient with the lowest plasma viral load is minimal and vice versa.
NK activity and expression of NK receptors of HIV‐infected patients with the lowest viral loads are significantly lower and higher, respectively, compared to HIV‐infected and HIV‐negative controls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the modulation of expression of NK receptors of cytolytic effector cells in relation to the viral burden in HIV/AIDS.
the role of NK receptors on the effector functions of NK and cytolytic cells.
the role of the NK cell in HIV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

HIV‐infected individuals, particularly those with high viral loads and low CD4+ T cell counts, have a compromised innate immunity, which may be due to the down‐regulation of NK activity and/or the expression of MHC class I binding NK receptors.

HIV infection leads to a significant decrease in NK cell activity and that this decrease is associated with the expression of MHC class I molecules on the cell surface of HIV‐infected cells and the modulation of NK receptor expression on NK cells.
the NK cell activity is decreased in HIV‐inflected patients, and this decrease is related to viral replication.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NK cell activity is inversely related to the viral load and the expression of the NK receptors are altered in HIV infection.
HIV infection leads to decreased NK activity and altered expression of NK receptors, both on CD8+ T cells and on CD56+ cells in relation to HIV load.
the NK activity of the patients with lowest plasma HIV load was minimal and vice versa suggesting a decrease in NK activity following suppression of the HIV replication.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NK cell activity of HIV‐infected patients was inversely related to viral load.
the NK cell activity is inversely proportional to the viral burden of HIV in the patients.
NK cells are a very important component of the immune response against HIV.
